excerpt: How to save a page so you can find it in a year, how to put bookmarks in folders, and which five links are worth pinning to the bar.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to save a web page and find it again months later. You will learn the star, the bookmarks bar, and folders inside it, and you will know which five pages deserve a place on the bar. If you have ever searched for your own bank twice a week, this fixes it.

A bookmark is a saved address with a name you choose. It saves the page, not a copy of it: if the page changes, the bookmark still opens the current version, which is what you want for a bank or a school portal.
Before you start

items: A browser open on a page you use often.
About ten minutes.

body.text: The star, the bar, and the menu
There are three places a bookmark can live, and knowing them stops the pile from becoming a mystery.

items: Click the star at the right end of the address bar. The page is saved at once.
A small box appears where you can change the name before you save.
Choose a folder in that box if you want to keep the bar tidy.
Show the bar with Ctrl, Shift and B, so one click opens the page.
Open the full list from the menu, under Bookmarks, when the bar is hidden.

body.text: You will see the star turn solid blue once the page is saved, and the page appear on the bar if you chose that folder. A hollow star means the page is not saved yet.

body.alt: A browser address bar with the bookmark star highlighted.
body.caption: The star saves the page. A solid star means it is saved, and a hollow one means it is not.

body.text: It looks like saving everything is harmless. A list of two hundred unsorted bookmarks is a list nobody opens, and it is how people end up searching for their own bank every week.
Folders, so you can find one
Five folders are enough for most people. Name them for what you do, not for what the sites are.

items: Right-click the bookmarks bar and choose Add folder.
Name them for your week: Money, School, Work, Reference, Later.
Right-click any bookmark and choose Edit to move it into a folder.
Keep the top level under about seven items, so every one is visible.
Delete a bookmark the moment you notice you never use it.

body.text: None of this is permanent. A folder takes a second to rename, and a tidy bar is easier to keep tidy than to rebuild.

body.alt: A browser bookmarks bar showing folders for money, school and work.
body.caption: Folders named for your week. Seven visible items beat two hundred hidden ones.

body.text: What to pin, and what not to
The bar is the most valuable space in the browser. Put on it only what you open weekly.

items: Your bank, reached by typing the address yourself the first time.
Your email, the school portal, and one work tool.
A reference page you use constantly, such as the academy notes.
Your own cloud folder, if you share links often.
Not: an article you might read one day. Save that in a Later folder instead.
Not: a site you reached from a link in a message, until you have checked the address.

body.text: Do not worry about losing bookmarks when you change phone or laptop. Signing in to the browser syncs them, as long as you are signed in before you switch machines.
If it goes wrong
Bookmarks are easy to recover, and the first fix solves most cases.

items: The bar disappeared: press Ctrl, Shift and B to bring it back.
You saved a page with a useless name: right-click it and choose Edit.
A bookmark opens the wrong page: the site changed its address. Delete it and save the page again.
All bookmarks vanished after a reset: sign in to the browser profile and let sync restore them.
You clicked a saved link and landed somewhere odd: the site was sold or the address expired. Delete the bookmark and find the official page yourself.
Too many bookmarks to manage: export them once from the menu, then start the bar again with five.

body.text: Practice
Five minutes and the bar becomes useful rather than decorative.

items: Save the page you visit most, with a name you would say out loud.
Show the bookmarks bar and confirm the page appears on it.
Make two folders, Money and School, and move one bookmark into each.
Delete one bookmark you have not opened this month.
Save one reference page into a Later folder rather than the bar.

body.text: You can now get to the pages that matter in one click. In the next lesson you will use the browser's memory of where you have been, and understand what a private window really hides.

excerpt: How to find a page you visited last Tuesday, what browser history keeps, what a private window does and does not hide, and when to clear history.

body.text: This lesson explains browser history and private windows. You will find a page you visited but did not save, understand what a private window actually hides, and know when clearing history is the right thing to do. Neither feature is a secret, and neither one is dangerous.
History is a list of pages your browser has visited, with the time and the title. It is a diary kept for your convenience, and it is stored on the machine, not on the websites.
Before you start

items: A browser you have used for a few days.
About ten minutes.

body.text: Find last Tuesday
You rarely need the whole list. You need one page you saw once and did not save, and history finds it in four clicks.

items: Press Ctrl and H to open history.
Search a word you remember from the page title.
Change the range, or scroll by date, if you know roughly when.
Click the entry to reopen the page.
Save it as a bookmark this time, so history is not needed again.

body.text: You will see a list grouped by day, with the newest at the top and a search box near the top of the page. Typing three letters narrows the list faster than scrolling.

body.alt: A browser history page listing sites by date.
body.caption: History is grouped by day. Search a word from the title instead of scrolling through weeks.

body.text: What private actually does
A private window, or incognito, keeps no history on that device when you close it. It is a clean table, not a mask.

items: It does not save history, cookies, or form entries after you close the window.
It does not hide what you do from your network, your internet provider, or your employer.
It does not make you anonymous to the websites you visit.
It does not protect you from viruses or from a link that steals a password.
It is useful on a shared machine, and for checking a second login to the same site.

body.text: It looks like a private window hides everything. It hides the trail on the device in front of you, and nothing else, which is why it is the right tool for a borrowed laptop and the wrong tool for anything illegal or dangerous.

body.alt: A private browsing window with the mask icon in the title bar.
body.caption: A private window keeps no trail on that device. It does not hide you from the network or from the site.

body.text: When to clear history
Clearing history is normal housekeeping, and it is also a reasonable thing to do before handing over a machine.

items: Clear before you sell, lend, or repair a computer.
Clear when the address bar keeps suggesting a page you no longer want.
Clear the last hour when you have been testing links and the list is a mess.
Do not clear if you are trying to find something: find it first, then clear.
Choose the range carefully, because All time removes everything.

body.text: None of this deletes bookmarks or files. History and cookies are separate, and clearing one does not clear the other unless you tick both.
If it goes wrong
History problems are small, and every case here has a plain fix.

items: A page you visited is missing from history: it was opened in a private window, or history was cleared.
Ctrl and H does nothing: the browser has a different shortcut. Use the menu, then History.
History is empty on a new machine: it lives on the old device unless the browser was synced.
You cleared history by mistake: it cannot be restored, but the pages may still appear in the address bar suggestions.
Somebody else can see your history: sign out of the browser profile, and use your own profile from now on.
A private window will not open: an extension or a workplace policy is blocking it. Ask before you work around it.

body.text: Practice
Find one real page today, and the feature stops being abstract.

items: Open history and find a page you visited this week.
Search history for a word rather than scrolling.
Open a private window, visit a site, close it, and confirm it is not in history.
Bookmark the page you found, so next time you do not need history.
Clear history for the last hour only, and check the rest is still there.

body.text: You can now retrace your own steps and understand what a private window really covers. In the next lesson you will clear the folder where every download lands.

excerpt: Why Downloads fills up, how to make a file land in the right folder the first time, and what to do when the folder is eating your disk space.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to control the Downloads folder instead of letting it grow. You will clear the pile, change where files land, and free space on a full disk. Downloads is the most cluttered folder on most computers, and it takes ten minutes to fix.

Every file the internet sends you lands in Downloads by default: forms, receipts, installers, photographs, and the same invoice you have saved four times under four names. It is a delivery mat, and nobody sweeps it.
You will see the folder marked with a down arrow in File Explorer's sidebar, usually holding more files than every other folder combined.
Before you start

items: File Explorer open on Downloads.
About fifteen minutes.
A folder in Documents called Archive, if you do not have one.

body.text: The five-minute walk
You do not need to sort every file. You need the folder to stop being the place where things go to be forgotten.

items: Open Downloads and switch to Details view.
Sort by Date modified so the newest appear first.
Open the newest ten and decide where each one belongs.
Move the ones you need into Documents, Pictures, or the Archive folder.
Delete the installers you have already used, and anything older than a year.
Leave nothing in Downloads that you would be sorry to lose.

body.text: You will see the folder shrink to a short list, and the disk space bar in This PC move a little. That movement is the reward, and it is the reason to repeat this once a month.

body.alt: A Downloads folder with mixed files sorted by date.
body.caption: Sort by date and deal with the newest ten. A folder of two hundred files is a week of small decisions, not one big one.

body.text: It looks like deleting an installer is a risk. An installer you have already used can be downloaded again, and the program it installed does not need it.
Make files land in the right room
Most browsers will ask where to save, if you tell them to. That one setting ends the pile at the source.

items: Open the browser settings and find Downloads.
Turn on Ask where to save each file before downloading.
From then on, name the file and choose the folder at the moment of saving.
Save documents into Documents, pictures into Pictures, and installers anywhere you will remember.
For a file you will only read once, choose Desktop and delete it afterwards.

body.text: None of this slows you down. It moves one small decision from next month to this minute, when you still remember what the file is.

body.alt: A person sorting downloaded files into folders on a laptop.
body.caption: Ask where to save, and name the file while you still know what it is. That is the whole method.

body.text: The name with a one in brackets
When you download the same file twice, the browser adds a number, and you end up with invoice.pdf, invoice (1).pdf, and invoice (2).pdf, none of which tells you which is current.

items: Rename the newest one with the date: invoice-october-2026.pdf.
Delete the older copies once you have checked the new one opens.
Open the file before you delete the others, to confirm it is complete.
Keep one copy in the right folder, not three in Downloads.

body.text: Do not worry about keeping every version of a form. Keep the one you submitted, and let the earlier drafts go.
If it goes wrong
A full disk causes real problems, and each one here has a clear next step.

items: The disk is full: clear Downloads first, then the Recycle Bin, then old videos.
A file will not delete because it is in use: close the program that opened it, or restart.
You deleted something you needed: check the Recycle Bin before anything else.
Downloads vanished from the sidebar: it is still in This PC, under your user folder.
The browser will not ask where to save: the setting is off, or a workplace policy fixed the folder.
A download never finishes: pause and resume, or try again on a stronger connection.

body.text: Practice
One pass today, and a reminder on the first of each month.

items: Sort Downloads by date and deal with the newest ten files.
Turn on Ask where to save in the browser settings.
Download one file and watch it ask for a folder.
Delete the installers you no longer need.
Check the free space on your drive before and after.

body.text: You can now keep the delivery mat clear and the disk healthy. In the next lesson you will meet the folder in the sky that everyone mentions but few explain.

excerpt: What cloud storage actually is, what it costs, how to use it without losing access to your own files, and when it is not a backup.

body.text: This lesson explains cloud storage in ordinary words: what it is, what it costs, and how to use it without depending on it completely. You will upload one folder, open it on a second device, and know the case where the cloud is not a backup.

The cloud is somebody else's computer holding a copy of your files. When you open a cloud folder, your device downloads the copy or streams it. The files are not in the air; they are on a server in a data centre, and you reach them through the internet.
Before you start

items: An account with Google Drive, OneDrive, or iCloud.
One folder with a few documents in it.
About twenty minutes, and enough data to upload it.

body.text: What it is for
The cloud solves three problems: reaching your files from another device, sharing a file with somebody without email limits, and surviving a stolen laptop.

items: Upload the folders you need on more than one device.
Share a single file with a link rather than sending thirty attachments.
Open a document on a phone to read it, and edit it on a laptop later.
Keep the free plan until you actually need more space.
Check the price in naira before you upgrade, because it is charged monthly.

body.text: You will see a small tick or an arrow beside a file name once the upload finishes, and a progress bar while it is going. A file with a cloud icon but no tick is not safely uploaded yet, and closing the lid can interrupt it.

body.alt: A cloud storage folder open with files and upload ticks.
body.caption: A tick beside the name means the copy reached the server. That is the difference between a file on your disk and a file you can reach anywhere.

body.text: It looks like the cloud keeps everything safely forever. Free accounts are closed after long periods without signing in, and a forgotten password can lock you out of your own files.
The free rooms and the paid house
Every provider gives a small amount free, usually fifteen gigabytes on Google, five on Microsoft, and five on Apple. That is enough for documents, and not enough for video.

items: Count your space: documents take kilobytes, photographs take megabytes, videos take gigabytes.
Delete the videos from the cloud before you pay for more room.
Keep a backup of the password and the recovery phone number for the account itself.
Check whether upgrading is monthly or yearly before you click.
Do not use a school or workplace account for personal files: the school can close it.

body.text: None of this costs anything to try. The free tier is enough for the documents most people actually need to reach from two places.

body.alt: A phone and a laptop showing the same cloud folder.
body.caption: One folder, two devices. The cloud is a copy that travels, not a copy that replaces the ones you hold.

body.text: Not a backup until it is a second house
A cloud folder is a copy, and one copy is not a backup. If you delete the file on your laptop and the folder syncs, the copy in the cloud is deleted too.

items: Keep at least two copies: one on a device you own, one in the cloud or on a drive.
Use version history to recover a file you overwrote, in the provider's menu.
Check the trash in the cloud service, which keeps deleted files for about thirty days.
Keep the important folders on a flash drive as well, once a month.
Write the account password down, because losing access is the same as losing the files.

body.text: Do not worry about the cloud being unsafe in general. The real risks are a forgotten password, a closed free account, and a delete that syncs everywhere at once.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a recovery path, and the first two solve most of them.

items: A file is missing from the cloud: check the service's trash, then the version history.
Uploads never finish: check the connection, then upload one file at a time.
The account is full: delete large videos and empty the trash.
You cannot sign in: use the recovery phone number, and check the account's own help pages.
Files disappeared from the laptop after you deleted them in the cloud: restore them from the cloud trash.
A shared link lets anyone edit your folder: change the link setting to view only, and re-share.

body.text: Practice
Upload one folder today, and open it on a phone to prove it works.

items: Sign in to your cloud account and check how much space is free.
Upload one folder of documents and wait for the ticks.
Open one file on a phone.
Share a file with yourself by link, then change it to view only.
Write the account password in your notebook, next to the recovery number.

body.text: You can now use the cloud as a travelling copy without depending on it entirely. In the next lesson you will leave a machine that is not yours without leaving anything behind.

excerpt: The five-minute checklist before you walk away from a borrowed or business-centre computer, what normally gets left behind, and how to undo it if you forgot.

body.text: This lesson is the checklist to run before you walk away from a computer that is not yours: a business centre, a friend's laptop, a school lab, or an office desk. You will learn what to close, what to sign out of, and what to do if you realise later that you did not.
A shared machine remembers you in more places than you expect: the browser session, the saved password, the Downloads folder, and the account that stays signed in to Windows itself.
Before you start

items: Two minutes now, and this page open on your phone if you can.
A note of any account you signed in to while you were there.

body.text: The five-minute walk
Do these in order. The last one is the one people forget, and it matters most.

items: Sign out of every website, using the account menu, not just by closing the tab.
Close the browser completely.
Delete the files you downloaded and empty the Recycle Bin.
Clear the browser history and cookies if the browser belongs to somebody else.
Sign out of the Windows or macOS account, or switch the machine off.
Unplug your flash drive using Eject, and take it with you.

body.text: You will see the browser return to a sign-in page and the account name disappear from the top corner. If the name is still there, the sign-out did not finish.

body.alt: A browser account menu with the sign out option highlighted.
body.caption: Sign out from the account menu. Closing the tab leaves the session open for the next person.

body.text: It looks like closing the browser signs you out. It usually does not, because the session is stored as a cookie that survives until it expires or you clear it.
The account that remembers the machine
On Windows, the computer itself may remember your email account, and the next person can see the name on the sign-in screen. On a business centre machine, that is worth avoiding.

items: Before you use a borrowed machine, ask whether you can use a guest account.
If you must sign in to Windows, use a local account rather than your personal email account.
Remove your account from the machine afterwards, in Settings, then Accounts.
Check the sign-in screen again after you remove it.
On a shop computer, do not sign in to Windows at all. Work in the browser and use a private window.

body.text: None of this is about being suspicious of the person beside you. A business centre machine is used by strangers all day, and the person after you is a stranger too.

body.alt: A person standing up to leave a business centre computer.
body.caption: Two minutes before you stand up: sign out, close, delete, clear. Then leave.

body.text: What still leaks
Some things survive a sign-out, and knowing them is what makes the checklist realistic rather than magical.

items: Files left in Downloads survive until somebody deletes them.
A printed page stays in the tray or beside the printer.
The printer's own memory may keep the last document you printed.
A remembered password stays if you clicked Save.
A session on a phone app that was signed in while you worked stays signed in.

body.text: Do not worry about being perfect. Signing out, deleting your files, and taking your flash drive removes almost all of the risk.
If it goes wrong
You can still act after you leave, and the first two steps are the ones that matter.

items: You forgot to sign out of email: change the password now, which ends the session, then sign out of other devices.
You left a file on the machine: call the centre and ask them to delete it, then treat the file as seen.
You saved a password on a shared machine: change that password today.
You left a flash drive behind: go back for it, and if you cannot, change any password written on it.
You left a printed page with your details: call and ask them to destroy it.
You are not sure what you signed in to: change the password on the two accounts that matter most, email and bank.

body.text: Practice
Run the checklist once on your own machine, so it becomes automatic.

items: Sign out of one site and watch the account name disappear.
Delete a file and empty the Recycle Bin.
Clear history for the last hour only.
Eject a flash drive properly and remove it.
Write the checklist in your notebook, with the six steps in order.

body.text: You can now use a borrowed computer and leave nothing of yourself behind. The next chapter begins the part of the series that protects all of this: accounts, permissions, and privacy.
